posts.text:
the first 30 seconds of a sales call matter more than the next 30 minutes.
 
I know that sounds extreme. but think about it.
 
if you open with "thanks for taking the time, let me share a quick overview of what we do" - the prospect has already decided what kind of call this is. polite. predictable. forgettable.
 
but if you open with something specific about their company, a problem you think they have, something that makes them stop and think - everything shifts.
 
they lean in. they start talking. they tell you things they probably weren't planning to share.
 
the best calls I've ever had didn't start with a pitch or an agenda. they started with one sentence that made the prospect feel like I actually did my homework.
 
after that, the next 30 minutes take care of themselves.

what makes or breaks a sales call - the opening or the close?

Claude Fable 5 replaced my entire LinkedIn outbound workflow.

Not "helps me."

It actually runs it.

To be clear, Claude can't do this by itself.

I connected it to one tool, and that combination replaced almost my entire outbound stack.

Here's what it does:

→ Finds prospects from real buying signals like hiring, funding, job changes, and competitor engagement.

→ I type a company name, it finds the right decision-maker, enriches the profile, and gets everything ready. No Apollo. No CRM hopping.

→ Every message is written from the prospect's real activity, not from a generic template.

→ It handles replies, qualifies prospects, and books meetings automatically.

→ I can ask questions like "Which job titles replied the most this week?" and it gives me the answer instantly.

No workflow builders.

No 20-step automations.

No jumping between five different tools.

I just chat with Claude, and it handles the rest.

The whole setup took less than 5 minutes.

Comment "TOOL" and I'll send you the exact setup.

I sent a prospect the same email three times in one week.

Copy. Paste. Send.

Nothing.

Fourth time I deleted the template.

Opened his company page.

They had just launched a new product.

I wrote three lines about it and hit send.

He replied before lunch.

Same guy who ghosted me all week.

The difference wasn't the writing.

Something had happened at his company that week.

My first three emails landed on a normal Tuesday.

The fourth landed two days after a launch.

I didn't write a better email. I hit a better week.

So I stopped picking follow-up dates.

Now the trigger picks them.

A prospect posts three new SDR roles. lemlist flags it that day.

The sequence fires the LinkedIn message I wrote for exactly that signal:
"Saw you're building the team. What's breaking first, sourcing or follow-up?"

I wrote that line once. It goes out every time the signal fires.

Only last month: 20 signal-triggered messages. 35% reply rate.

I don't decide when to follow up anymore.

The signal does.

Do you rewrite every follow-up or keep sending the same one?

#lemlistpartner

I stopped sending cold emails after lunch.

For years I just sent them whenever.

Between meetings. After lunch. End of day.

I did the same thing for months.

Then I saw the data.

Smartlead analyzed 850 million cold emails sent in H1 2026.

850 million.

The result was clear.

7am sends outperform everything else.

Sending in the afternoon takes roughly 60% more effort for the same number of replies.

I was working harder for worse results and I had no idea.

So I moved everything to the morning.

Same emails. Same sequences. Same copy.

More replies.

That was just one finding.

The full report covers where you actually rank against every other sender on the platform.

It's free.

Comment "REPORT" and I'll send it to you.

you've all been working remotely for years. you just didn't realize it.
 
look at this building. hundreds of people, multiple floors, different rooms. looks like the opposite of remote work right?
 
now think about what actually happens inside.
 
need something from finance? you send a slack message. need your manager? you call them. need a file from the team on the third floor? you don't walk up there. you send an email.
 
nobody walks anywhere. nobody knocks on doors. everyone's sitting in the same building talking through a screen.
 
that's not office work. that's remote work with a commute.
 
are you for remote work or in office?
